::: {.why}
The same estimation-error argument from week 15 applies to combining signals, with the additional problem that signal information coefficients are estimated even more noisily than asset means.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Report the out-of-sample performance of three combination schemes and say which won.
- State the condition under which optimised signal weights beat equal weights, and check it on your data.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Run the comparison out of sample rather than in: fit weights on the first part of the sample and evaluate on the rest, for equal weighting, IC weighting and mean-variance weighting on the signal returns. Report all three with intervals, and repeat at three estimation window lengths.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Say when optimising wins: when the dispersion in true information coefficients across signals is large relative to their estimation error. Estimate both quantities for your own book and state which regime you are in. This is the same calculation as day 101 with signals in place of assets.
:::
:::

## Resources

- [Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2014) — ...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns](https://www.nber.org/papers/w20592) [paper]{.res-kind}
- [skfolio — scikit-learn compatible portfolio optimization](https://skfolio.org/) [tool]{.res-kind}

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
Three combination schemes compared out of sample at three window lengths, with the dispersion-versus-error condition evaluated.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
You have two signals with the same IC and correlation 0.8. How do you weight them, and what happens as the correlation approaches 1?
:::
